paper_metadata.title: Provable bounds for noise-free expectation values computed from noisy samples

summary: The paper studies noise-robust sampling and CVaR bounds for gate-based quantum circuits, demonstrating them on IBM ibm_sherbrooke with QAOA. It reports a 40-qubit MAXCUT experiment at depths p=1,2 with 10^5 and 10^7 shots, and a 127-qubit higher-order Ising experiment at depths p=1..5 with 10^5 shots each; in the latter, noisy expectation values improve from -64.54 to -85.78 while the noise-free MPS references range from -79.79 to -145.54, and the best sampled values reach -136 to -164 versus a global optimum of -188.

experiments.description: QAOA for MAXCUT on a random 3-regular graph with 40 nodes, executed on IBM ibm_sherbrooke at depths p=1 and p=2; classical light-cone optimization used to set angles and evaluate noise-free reference values.

algorithm.optimizer: classical light-cone optimization / parameter optimization (method not specified)
algorithm.parameter_initialization: classically optimized angles from light-cone simplification; exact initialization method not otherwise specified

problem_formulation.encoding_details: MAXCUT on 3-regular graph mapped to Ising/QUBO form with 1 qubit per graph node
problem_formulation.objective_function: maximize cut value (equivalently minimize Ising energy for MAXCUT)
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: MAXCUT Ising Hamiltonian (not explicitly written in the excerpt)

problem_instance.description: Random 3-regular graph MAXCUT instance from Ref. [11]

dataset_specification.description: 40-node random 3-regular graph; instance taken from Ref. [11]

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: none reported beyond light-cone simplification for classical evaluation of expectation values
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: circuits run on hardware; 10^5 shots for p=1 and 10^7 shots for p=2; compare noisy expectation, noise-free expectation from classical light-cone simulation, CVaR, best sampled value, and global optimum

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise; Pauli-Lindblad model / layer-fidelity characterization; no twirling in main experiments
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: CVaR-based bounds; staggered dynamical decoupling; layer fidelity analysis

implementation_details.mitigation_details: staggered dynamic decoupling applied; CVaR evaluated on noisy samples; no twirling in main experiments
implementation_details.transpilation_target: CNOT layers mapped to ECR-native IBM hardware
implementation_details.classical_solver: CPLEX used only for optimal solution reference in other section, not this experiment
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: classical light-cone optimization to compute angles and reference expectation values
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: sort samples and compute CVaR over best alpha fraction; compare to noisy expectation and best sampled value

speedup_claims.factor: sampling overhead reduced from O(gamma^2) to O(sqrt(gamma))
speedup_claims.conditions: for extracting good samples / CVaR-based bounds on noisy samples
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a bound on sampling overhead, not a proven computational speedup; PEC gives unbiased expectation estimates but with larger overhead.

speedup_claims.factor: provable performance guarantees for QAOA on MAXCUT recovered under noisy hardware with sqrt(gamma) sampling overhead
speedup_claims.conditions: for MAXCUT on 3-regular graphs, using CVaR with alpha <= 1/sqrt(gamma)
speedup_claims.caveats: Guarantees are about approximation ratios / bounds, not asymptotic runtime advantage.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: QAOA with p=1,2; no asymptotic complexity claim beyond sampling overhead scaling
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: classical light-cone simulation up to 14 qubits for expectation evaluation

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 40-qubit QAOA on ibm_sherbrooke with p=1,2; 10^5 and 10^7 shots; classical light-cone simulation used for reference values
limiting_factors: No classical runtime comparison showing quantum advantage
Sampling overhead from noise is large (reported sqrt(gamma) values 735 and 540275.9)
Classical light-cone simulation still provides the reference values
Problem is a benchmark MAXCUT instance, not a demonstrated practical application

notes: num_qubits inferred from 40-node graph and explicit statement that the experiment is on 40 qubits.
circuit_depth reported as QAOA depths p=1 and p=2; gate counts and shot counts are explicitly stated in the paper.
speedup_order set to none_proven because the paper discusses performance guarantees and sampling overhead, not an asymptotic quantum speedup over classical methods.
The paper reports approximation ratios and CVaR bounds, but no claim of quantum advantage over classical methods.
Classical simulation is used to obtain noise-free expectations and optimal angles.

experiments.description: QAOA on a hardware-efficient higher-order Ising spin-glass model with 127 variables, executed on IBM ibm_sherbrooke for depths p=1 to p=5; parameters transferred from smaller instances and validated with MPS simulation and CPLEX optimum reference.

algorithm.variant: QAOA for higher-order Ising spin-glass models on heavy-hex hardware
algorithm.optimizer: parameter transfer / heuristic angle selection (no on-device variational optimization reported)
algorithm.parameter_initialization: heuristic angles obtained via parameter transfer from same-structure problems; exact initial values not listed in the excerpt

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 1 qubit per binary variable on a heavy-hex-compatible graph; linear, quadratic, and cubic Ising terms encoded via parity computation/uncomputation on data qubits
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimize the higher-order Ising Hamiltonian; the paper frames it as a random coefficient spin glass problem
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H = sum_v d_v Z_v + sum_(i,j) d_{i,j} Z_i Z_j + sum_l d_{l,n1(l),n2(l)} Z_l Z_{n1(l)} Z_{n2(l)}

problem_instance.description: Random hardware-compatible higher-order Ising spin-glass instance on a heavy-hex graph

dataset_specification.description: 127-qubit heavy-hex-compatible graph; coefficients for linear, quadratic, and cubic terms chosen uniformly from {+1,-1}

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: each p run on ibm_sherbrooke with 10^5 shots; compare noisy expectation, noise-free expectation from MPS simulation, best sampled value, and fitted CVaR alpha values; bootstrap used to estimate CVaR variance

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise; layer-fidelity characterization; no twirling in main experiments
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: CVaR-based bounds; staggered dynamic decoupling; bootstrap variance study

implementation_details.mitigation_details: staggered dynamic decoupling applied; CVaR bounds discussed but analytic shot requirements deemed impractical; bootstrap over 10^5 sampled values repeated 10^4 times to estimate CVaR variance
implementation_details.transpilation_target: IBM heavy-hex superconducting device with ECR native gates; paper reports CNOT-equivalent counts
implementation_details.classical_solver: CPLEX used to compute optimal solutions for the Ising instances
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: parameter transfer and MPS simulation to validate angles; CPLEX for optimum
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: CVaR estimation from sorted samples; bootstrap variance estimation

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: noisy expectation improves from p=1 to p=4 and worsens at p=5

speedup_claims.factor: sampling overhead reduced from O(gamma^2) to O(sqrt(gamma))
speedup_claims.conditions: for CVaR-based bounds on noisy samples
speedup_claims.caveats: Analytic CVaR bounds were stated to require impractically many shots for this 127-qubit instance; the paper instead validates variance scaling via bootstrap.

speedup_claims.factor: provable bounds on noise-free expectation values from noisy samples
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a bound, not an unbiased estimator.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: QAOA with CNOT depth 6p per round on heavy-hex-compatible higher-order Ising models
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: MPS simulation with bond dimension chi=2048; CPLEX used for optimum reference

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 127-qubit QAOA on ibm_sherbrooke for p=1..5; 10^5 shots per depth; MPS simulation and CPLEX used as classical references
limiting_factors: No classical runtime comparison showing quantum advantage
Analytic CVaR shot requirements are described as impractical
Classical CPLEX computes the optimum and MPS validates the circuit outputs
No evidence that the quantum device beats classical optimization on this instance

notes: Circuit depth inferred from the paper's statement that each QAOA round has CNOT depth 6 and p=1..5, giving depths 6,12,18,24,30.
num_qubits reported as 127 qubits/variables in the paper.
speedup_order set to none_proven because the paper focuses on noise robustness and scaling of sampling overhead, not a quantum advantage claim.
The paper reports improved noisy expectation values with increasing p and compares against classical MPS/CPLEX references, but does not demonstrate advantage.
